4.title: Stewards of Grace: The Meaning of Suffering
4.overview: Chapter 4 returns to the theme of suffering but with a new theological frame: the end of all things is at hand (v. 7), so suffering must be understood eschatologically. The first half (vv. 1–11) grounds the break with the old life and the obligations of the new community in the nearness of the end. The second half (vv. 12–19) addresses the 'fiery trial' directly: do not be surprised by it; it is the expected furnace-testing of the gospel age; rejoice to share Christ's sufferings; and commit yourselves to the faithful Creator. The chapter is the letter's most direct pastoral address to a suffering community.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Stewards of God's Varied Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin (v.1), so as to live the rest of the time for the will of God rather than human passions (v.2). The past time is enough for sensuality, drunkenness and lawless idolatry (v.3); the neighbours are astonished that you no longer join the flood, and malign you (v.4) — but they will answer to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead (v.5). This is why the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead: though judged in the flesh as people are, they might live in the spirit as God does (v.6).

The end of all things is at hand, so be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers (v.7). Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins (v.8). Show hospitality without grumbling (v.9). As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another as good stewards of God's varied grace (v.10) — whoever speaks, as one speaking oracles of God; whoever serves, by the strength God supplies — so that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ (v.11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Stewards of God's Varied Grace

Suffering for Christ settles a believer's break with sin. Because the end is near, stay clear-headed for prayer, love earnestly, and use each gift to serve others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Neighbours were surprised when converts no longer joined them, and they spoke against them.

Now: Love covers a multitude of sins: it does not pass offences around.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Arm yourselves with the same way of thinking.' The verb is a soldier's word — take up your weapons — and what Peter hands them is not a shield but a thought. The armament is mental: the settled conviction that suffering is the road Christ took.

That is a realistic piece of pastoral care. A Christian ambushed by suffering he did not expect is far more likely to collapse than one who decided in advance what it means. Peter is telling them to make the decision before the trial rather than during it.

Then the difficult clause: 'whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin.' Read flatly it seems to say that suffering makes a person sinless, which is plainly untrue and contradicts the commands that follow.

Two readings carry weight. It may refer to Christ himself — he suffered and is now done with sin, having dealt with it once for all (3:18). Or, more likely given the 'whoever', it describes what suffering does to a believer's relationship with sin. The man who has genuinely paid a price for following Christ has made a decisive break: he has already chosen, under pressure, and the choosing settles something.

Verse 2 supports the second reading by stating the result: 'so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.' The break is about direction, not perfection. Something has been finished with.

Anyone who has suffered for a conviction knows the effect. Once you have lost something real for Christ, the appeal of what you gave up is permanently reduced — you have already found out what it was worth. That is not sinlessness. It is a man who has stopped negotiating.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For the time that is past suffices.' The understatement is almost dry — you have given that quite enough of your life already. Peter does not argue them out of their old habits; he simply says the account is closed.

Then six words for what they had left, and the list is unsparing: sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. These were not abstractions. Much of it was religious — the temple feasts of a Greek city ran on exactly this, and the last item names what held the rest together.

Note that the whole list is social. Every item is something done in company, which is precisely why leaving it cost these people their friends.

'With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them.' The verb means to be taken aback, thrown by something unaccountable. Their neighbours are genuinely puzzled — not offended on principle but bewildered that anyone would opt out.

'The same flood of debauchery' is a vivid word: an outpouring, a torrent, something running out of its channel. And the picture explains the reaction. When everyone is being carried along by a current, the person standing still is not merely different — he is an implied criticism of everyone moving past him.

Does this mean Christians should avoid social occasions with unbelievers altogether? No. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners (Luke 7:34), and Paul says we cannot leave the world (1 Cor 5:9–10). Peter warns against joining in the excesses: drunkenness, orgies, idolatry. A Christian may be at the party; he should not be part of what the party becomes.

'And they malign you.' That is the mechanism of the slander this whole letter addresses. It does not begin in theological objection. It begins in social withdrawal: you stopped coming, and the people you stopped coming to have drawn their own conclusions about why.

verseByVerse.quote: but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.' The answer to being maligned is not vindication now but a court later — the same move as 2:23, where Christ entrusted himself to the one who judges justly.

'Ready' is the sharp word. Not eventually, not one day. He is standing by, prepared, and the delay is patience rather than absence.

Then verse 6, another genuinely disputed sentence: 'this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead.'

The most likely reading, and the one that fits the argument, is that these are Christians who have since died — people who heard the gospel while alive and are now dead. That was a live pastoral problem: believers had been dying, sometimes under persecution, and the obvious taunt from neighbours was that their faith had done them no good at all.

The verse answers exactly that. 'Though judged in the flesh the way people are' — they died, which is the judgement all flesh comes under — 'they might live in the spirit the way God does.' The verdict of death was passed on them as it is on everyone. It was not the last word.

The alternative reading, that the gospel is preached to the already-dead offering a second chance, cannot stand: it contradicts Hebrews 9:27 and empties the urgency of the New Testament's own preaching. And it is not needed, because the natural reading is both simpler and more comforting.

Does this offer a second chance after death? Some early writers read it as preaching to the dead in Hades; others link it to 3:19. The more likely reading is that the gospel was preached to believers while they were alive, who have since died; though they suffered judgment in the flesh, they live with God. Scripture offers no second chance after death (Heb 9:27).

So the pastoral force is this. A congregation burying its members under slander is told that death is the judgement everybody receives in the flesh, and that it settles nothing about the verdict that matters.

verseByVerse.quote: The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The end of all things is at hand.' The word for end is telos — not merely the stopping but the goal, the point everything has been heading for. Peter is not announcing that things will run out; he is saying they will arrive.

And 'at hand' has drawn a great deal of comment, since two thousand years have passed. The New Testament's consistent posture is not a calculated date but a nearness that makes everything urgent. Peter himself writes that with the Lord a day is as a thousand years (2 Pet 3:8), so he was not making a prediction he could be caught out by.

What matters is what he draws from it, and it is startling. Given that the end is near, you might expect a call to dramatic action — evangelise harder, wind up your affairs, gather on a hillside. Peter says: be self-controlled and sober-minded, and pray.

One of these words has appeared already. Sober-minded is from 1:13 — clear-headed, unintoxicated, seeing things as they are. Self-controlled is its companion. Peter's answer to eschatological urgency is a steady head.

'For the sake of your prayers.' And there is the purpose, which is the surprising part. The clear head is not for its own sake or for better decisions. It is so that they can pray — because a mind that is agitated, frightened or intoxicated cannot.

That is worth taking personally. Most people's prayer life fails not through unbelief but through mental clutter, and Peter treats the clearing of the head as a discipline undertaken specifically so that prayer becomes possible again.

verseByVerse.quote: Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Above all, keep loving one another earnestly.' The priority is stated plainly, and 'earnestly' is the stretched-out word from 1:22 — love at full extension, the effort of a muscle under strain.

'Since love covers a multitude of sins.' The phrase comes from Proverbs 10:12: hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offences. And 'covers' must be read rightly. This is not concealment of wrongdoing, and it is not the covering that atones — only Christ's blood does that.

It means love does not spread things. It refuses to publish, to relitigate, to keep the account open. A congregation of a dozen households under persecution, meeting weekly in someone's front room, will generate friction constantly; and the difference between a church that survives that and one that tears itself apart is whether small offences get covered or circulated.

Then verse 9, and it follows for a very practical reason: 'Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.'

Hospitality was not optional in that world. There were no church buildings — the congregation met in a home, and somebody's floor took the wear. Travelling Christians needed lodging, since inns were expensive and often disreputable. Peter's word means love-of-strangers, and it was a costly practical burden borne by whoever had the largest room.

Does love covers a multitude of sins mean we should keep quiet about serious sin, abuse or crime? No. Love overlooks many small offences and forgives readily. But serious or unrepentant sin is to be confronted (Matt 18:15–17; Gal 6:1), and abuse and crime must be reported to the proper authorities (Rom 13:4). Covering sin in love never means hiding harm from those who need protecting.

Which is exactly why 'without grumbling' is attached. Peter knows that the household hosting the church is the household most likely to resent it, and that the resentment will come out as muttering rather than refusal. The command is not to open your door — they were already doing that. It is to stop complaining about the cost of it.

verseByVerse.quote: As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As each has received a gift.' Each — the word carries the weight. Peter assumes that every member of these scattered congregations has been given something, and there is no category of Christian who has not.

'Use it to serve one another.' The gift is not for the possessor. It arrives already assigned, and the direction is toward other people — which settles the question of what gifts are for before anyone can make them a measure of standing.

'As good stewards of God's varied grace.' A steward manages what belongs to somebody else, and will be asked about it. And varied is a lovely word — literally many-coloured, used of an embroidered cloth. God's grace is not issued in one shade; the congregation is a fabric of different colours, and a single-coloured church has lost something God intended to be seen.

Then Peter divides all gifts into two: 'whoever speaks' and 'whoever serves'. Word and deed, and both are needed.

'As one who speaks oracles of God.' That is a weighty standard. Not that every Christian's words are inspired, but that anyone speaking in the congregation should handle the responsibility as though delivering God's own utterances — carefully, and not casually.

'As one who serves by the strength that God supplies.' The verb is the choregos word — the wealthy citizen who funded a chorus and paid for everything it needed. The servant does not run on his own reserves.

Does whoever speaks include prophecy and tongues today? Peter divides the gifts into speaking and serving, and the speaking he has in mind is the church’s teaching, preaching and exhortation, handled as God’s word, not new revelation. Continuationists include prophecy here; the more likely reading is that those who speak in the church today speak as one who speaks oracles of God by faithfully passing on the words God has already given.

And the purpose gathers both: 'in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.' Which is why Peter breaks into doxology mid-letter. A man thinking about gifts rightly ends up talking about God rather than about gifts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Do not be surprised at the fiery trial that comes to test you, as though something strange were happening (v.12), but rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, so that you may be glad when his glory is revealed (v.13). If you are insulted for the name of Christ you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you (v.14).

Let none of you suffer as a murderer, thief, evildoer or meddler (v.15); but if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed but glorify God in that name (v.16). For it is time for judgement to begin at the household of God — and if with us, what of those who do not obey the gospel (v.17)? If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly (v.18)? Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good (v.19).
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement Beginning at Home

Do not be surprised by the fiery trial. To suffer as a Christian is no shame; entrust your soul to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 'Christian' was probably an outsiders' label, and Peter tells them to wear it.

Now: Make sure any suffering is for Christ's name, not for wrongdoing or meddling.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you.' The word for surprised is the one used in verse 4 of the pagans, who were taken aback that Christians would not join them. Peter turns it round: they are astonished at you; do not you be astonished at this.

'The fiery trial' is literally the burning — the word used of smelting metal, and it reaches back to 1:7 where faith is refined like gold. Peter has not changed his mind about what the fire is for.

'When it comes', not if. And 'to test you' names the purpose, which is the whole point of the sentence. A trial with a purpose is a different experience from a trial without one, though the heat is identical.

'As though something strange were happening to you.' There is the pastoral target. The danger is not the suffering but the interpretation — the conclusion that this is abnormal, that it means God has withdrawn, that other Christians somewhere are having an easier time and must be doing it better.

Peter's answer is that persecution is not a deviation from the Christian life but a normal feature of it. Which is a hard word and a strangely freeing one: a great deal of the pain of suffering is the suspicion that it should not be happening.

'But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings.' Note the careful measure — insofar as. Peter is not commanding joy in suffering generally, but in the specific portion of it that is genuinely a share in Christ's. And 'share' is the fellowship word: this is participation, not imitation.

'That you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.' The joy is not two joys but one, arriving in two instalments. What is begun now under the fire will be completed at the revelation — and the second verb is the exuberant one, the word for shouting gladness.

verseByVerse.quote: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed.' The Beatitude again, as in 3:14 — Peter keeps returning to a sermon he heard on a hillside.

Note the precision: for the name of Christ. Not for being difficult, or tactless, or socially awkward. Peter will make the distinction explicit in the very next verse, and he is careful never to let a Christian claim the blessing for trouble he brought on himself.

And insult is the specific form named. Not imprisonment or death at this stage — reviling, the ordinary daily contempt of neighbours. Which is what most Christians under pressure actually face, then and now: not a courtroom but a reputation quietly destroyed.

Then the reason, and it is one of the most remarkable statements in the letter: 'because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.'

The verb 'rests' is the one used in Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit of the LORD rests on the shoot from the stump of Jesse — a messianic text. Peter says the same Spirit settles on an insulted congregation in Bithynia.

And there is very likely an echo of the glory-cloud that rested on the tabernacle. The presence that filled the tent now rests on people being sworn at in the street.

Which inverts the whole appearance of things. The neighbours see a group whose reputation is in ruins. Peter says the visible shame is the outward face of an invisible glory, and that the Spirit is not merely with them despite the insults but is resting on them precisely there.

verseByVerse.quote: But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer.' Peter will not let the blessing of verse 14 be claimed by a Christian who has earned his trouble. The distinction has run through the letter (2:20; 3:17) and he states it once more, bluntly.

Then the fourth item, and it does not belong with the first three: 'or as a meddler.' The word appears nowhere else in Greek literature and Peter may have coined it; it means something like an overseer-of-other-people's-business.

Set beside murder and theft it is startling, and the placing is the point. Peter puts interfering in other people's affairs in a list with felonies — because in a small suspected minority, the busybody does real damage. A Christian who cannot keep out of his neighbours' business will generate hostility and then mistake it for persecution.

'Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed.' The word Christian appears only three times in the New Testament, and this is the only place a believer uses it of himself. It was coined at Antioch (Acts 11:26) and was almost certainly an outsiders' nickname — Christ-people, Christ-ites.

So Peter takes the label the neighbours were using as an insult and tells them to wear it. That is what he means by not being ashamed: the name is being thrown at them, and the instruction is to catch it.

'But let him glorify God in that name.' The shame is not merely to be endured but converted. The mockers supplied the word; the Christian is to make it an occasion of praise — which takes the sting out of an insult more completely than any denial could.
verseByVerse.note: “Christian” was first a nickname given by outsiders; it appears only three times in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And "If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?" Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God.' A startling sentence, and it reframes everything the letter has described.

The idea is Ezekiel's. When judgement fell on Jerusalem, the command was to begin at the sanctuary (Ezek 9:6) — God's own house first. Peter is saying that the suffering these congregations are enduring is not merely persecution from outside; it is the first movement of God's own sifting, and it begins with his people.

That is not a comfortable thought and it is a clarifying one. Their trials are not outside God's programme, and they are not evidence of his absence. He has started, and he has started at home.

'And if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God?' The argument runs from lesser to greater and Peter leaves it as a question, which is more forceful than a statement. If the household is going through this, the question answers itself — and the reader is left to do the arithmetic about his persecutors, which is a far more sobering thing than being told.

Verse 18 quotes Proverbs 11:31. 'Scarcely saved' does not mean saved by a narrow margin or barely enough grace. It means saved with difficulty — through fire, through the process this letter has been describing. Salvation is certain and the road to it is hard, and Peter has never pretended otherwise.

Then the conclusion, and it is the finest sentence in the chapter: 'Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.'

The verb entrust is the deposit word, and the thought is the one used of Christ in 2:23, handing his case to the just Judge. And the title chosen for God is exact: Creator, used of him nowhere else in the New Testament. A man handing over his soul is giving it back to the one who made it, and 'faithful' means the deposit will be there when he asks for it. Note also that the entrusting is done 'while doing good' — not instead of acting, but in the middle of it.

5.title: Humble Yourselves: Elders, Community, and the God of All Grace
5.overview: The final chapter gathers the letter's ethical threads into three movements: the elders who are to shepherd (vv. 1–5), the whole community that is to humble itself under God's mighty hand and resist the devil (vv. 6–11), and the closing greetings that locate the letter in Rome and identify its bearers (vv. 12–14). The climax is one of the most beautiful benedictions in the NT: the God of all grace who called you to his eternal glory in Christ will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you (v. 10). The letter that began with scattered exiles ends with the promise that the God who scattered nothing — who chose them before the foundation of the world — will bring everything to completion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Shepherd the Flock of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Peter exhorts the elders as a fellow elder, a witness of Christ's sufferings and a partaker in the glory to be revealed (v.1): shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight — not under compulsion but willingly, not for shameful gain but eagerly (v.2), not domineering but being examples to the flock (v.3). And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory (v.4).

Likewise the younger are to be subject to the elders; and all of them are to tie on humility toward one another, for God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (v.5).
verseByVerse.theology:
Three Temptations and Their Remedies

Elders are to shepherd God's flock willingly, eagerly and by example — not under compulsion, not for gain, not by domineering. The chief Shepherd is coming.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote to them as a fellow elder, not as an apostle.

Now: Everyone is to put on humility toward one another, because God gives grace to the humble.

verseByVerse.quote: So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, as well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed:
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder.' Consider what Peter does not say. He could have written 'as an apostle', and the letter opened that way (1:1). Addressing church leaders about how to lead, he sets the title down and takes the same chair they are sitting in.

Sympresbyteros — fellow elder — appears nowhere else in the New Testament. He seems to have made it for this sentence, and it is the credential he wants in play: not authority over them but experience alongside them.

'And a witness of the sufferings of Christ.' That is a claim only a handful of men could make, and it carries more than the fact of having been present. Peter had watched, from the courtyard, and had failed there. When he tells elders to shepherd the flock, the words come from the man who was told three times on a beach to feed the sheep, after denying he knew the Shepherd at all.

'As well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed.' The tenses are worth noticing. He was a witness of the sufferings; he is a partaker of a glory not yet revealed. Peter puts himself and them in exactly the same position — between a suffering already seen and a glory still coming — which is where this whole letter has located its readers since the first chapter.

And there may be a memory in that word. Peter had seen glory revealed once, on the mountain, and had wanted to build shelters and stay. He writes now as a man who knows the glory is real and that it is not yet time.

verseByVerse.quote: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight.' Two verbs, and they are the two words the New Testament uses for church leadership — shepherding and overseeing. Peter has already given both titles to Christ (2:25), which fixes the terms: these men are undershepherds, and the flock is not theirs.

'The flock of God that is among you' says it twice over. It belongs to God, and the elder is among it rather than above it.

Then three pairs, each a temptation and its remedy, and together they are the most searching description of pastoral motive in Scripture.

'Not under compulsion, but willingly.' The first danger is doing it because you have to — from duty, or because nobody else will, or because you cannot see how to stop. Peter adds 'as God would have you', which locates the willingness: not natural enthusiasm but a work taken up under God.

'Not for shameful gain, but eagerly.' Money, and Peter assumes elders were paid something or the warning would be pointless. The word for the alternative means wholeheartedly, with zeal — the opposite of a man calculating what the post returns.

'Not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.' The third is power, and it is the one that ruins most. The verb means to lord it over — the very word the Lord used when he said the rulers of the Gentiles do this, and 'it shall not be so among you' (Mark 10:42-43). Peter was in the room.

And the alternative is not weak leadership but a costlier kind: example. A man who leads by command need only be obeyed; a man who leads by example has to be worth copying, and that is a far harder standard to meet on a Tuesday.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And when the chief Shepherd appears.' The word archipoimen occurs nowhere else in the Greek Bible, and it settles the whole passage. There is one chief Shepherd, and every elder addressed here is under him.

It also answers the three temptations of the previous verse at their root. A man who genuinely believes the flock belongs to someone else, who is coming back, will not serve grudgingly, or for money, or by domineering — because none of those makes sense if you are minding somebody else's sheep and he is due home.

'You will receive the unfading crown of glory.' The crown is stephanos, the victor's wreath at the games rather than a royal diadem — a circle of leaves, and everyone watching knew how quickly it browned.

So Peter's adjective is chosen with care: unfading, amarantinos, from the amaranth, the flower the ancients used as a symbol of what does not wither. He used the same root of the inheritance in 1:4. The wreath handed to an athlete was dead within the week; this one is made of something else.

And note what the crown is made of: 'the crown of glory' — most likely meaning the crown that consists of glory, as 'crown of life' in James 1:12 means the crown which is life. The reward is not a decoration to wear but a share in the glory Peter has just said he is a partaker of.

Does Peter’s calling himself a fellow elder tell against the papacy? Roman Catholic teaching sees Peter as the first bishop of Rome with authority over the whole church (cf. Matt 16:18–19). Here Peter, writing probably from Rome (v. 13), places himself alongside the elders, not over them, and points them to Christ, the chief Shepherd. Nothing in his letters claims a supreme office or successors.

Which is a striking thing to promise elders in a persecuted network of house churches. Their work was unpaid or barely paid, unnoticed outside their own street, and dangerous. Peter tells them the recognition is coming from the only person whose opinion is final.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders.' Having addressed the leaders, Peter turns to those most likely to chafe under them. The word may mean younger in years or simply those not holding office; either way the instruction is the same posture the letter has asked of citizens, slaves and wives.

Then the scope widens and takes everyone in: 'Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another.'

The verb is unusual and vivid. It means to tie something on — it was used of the apron a slave fastened over his clothes before serving. Peter is telling the whole congregation to put on the servant's apron.

And of all the men who could have chosen that image, Peter is the one who had watched it happen. In the upper room the Lord rose from supper, laid aside his outer garments, tied a towel round himself, and washed their feet — and Peter had objected, loudly, and been told that unless he allowed it he had no part with him (John 13:4-8). The picture he reaches for here is one he originally refused.

'For God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.' The quotation is Proverbs 3:34, and James uses it too (Jas 4:6) — evidently a text the early church leaned on hard.

The word for opposes is military: to draw up in battle order against. God does not merely decline to help the proud; he takes the field opposite them. And grace, being a gift, can only be received by open hands — which is why humility is not one virtue among several here but the posture in which anything at all can be received.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Cast Your Anxieties, and Stand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Humble yourselves under God's mighty hand, so that at the proper time he may exalt you (v.6), casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (v.7). Be sober-minded and watchful: your adversary the devil prowls like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (v.8). Resist him, firm in faith, knowing the same sufferings are being experienced by the brotherhood throughout the world (v.9).

And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you (v.10). To him be the dominion forever (v.11). Peter has written briefly by Silvanus, declaring that this is the true grace of God — stand firm in it (v.12). The church at Babylon, likewise chosen, greets them, and so does Mark (v.13). Greet one another with the kiss of love; peace to all who are in Christ (v.14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Why Worry Is Treated as Pride

Humble yourselves by casting all your anxieties on God, because he cares for you. After a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The devil prowled like a roaring lion, looking for anyone cut off from the flock.

Now: Resist him firm in the faith, knowing the same sufferings are shared by believers throughout the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God.' The 'therefore' follows the proverb: since that is how God deals with pride and humility, put yourself on the right side of it.

'The mighty hand of God' is an exodus phrase — it is how the Old Testament describes God bringing Israel out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. And it cuts both ways, which is why it is the right image here. The hand is heavy; it is also the hand that delivers.

'So that at the proper time he may exalt you.' The lifting is his work and his timing. Peter has already used kairos, the appointed moment, of God's dealings; a man who insists on being raised now has taken the job out of the right hands.

Then verse 7, and the grammar matters more than most readers realise. 'Casting all your anxieties on him' is not a separate command. It is a participle attached to 'humble yourselves' — the casting is how the humbling is done.

That connection is easily missed and it is the heart of the verse. We do not usually think of worry as pride. Peter does: holding on to your anxieties is a way of insisting that the situation is yours to manage, and handing them over is an act of self-lowering.

'Casting' is a decisive verb — throw it, the word used of the disciples flinging their cloaks on the colt (Luke 19:35). Not setting down gently, and not sharing. And 'all' leaves no category too small to bother him with.

Is anxiety a sin? This verse is an invitation, not a rebuke: he cares for you. Some anxiety comes from pride and self-reliance, and needs to be cast on God in humility (v. 6). But some anxiety has bodily causes and is an illness, and seeking help from a doctor or counsellor, or taking medication, is no lack of faith. Bring the burden to God, again and again, and use every means he provides.

'Because he cares for you.' The ground of the whole thing, and it is not that he is capable but that he is concerned. The word means it matters to him. Peter is writing to people whose neighbours had decided they were nothing, and the last word of the sentence is that they are on somebody's mind.

verseByVerse.quote: Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Be sober-minded; be watchful.' Two sharp imperatives, and the first has appeared before (1:13; 4:7). Peter's repeated counsel to a frightened church is a clear head and open eyes.

The second word is the one from Gethsemane — watch and pray (Matt 26:41) — where Peter did neither and slept. He is not issuing a command he has never failed.

'Your adversary the devil.' Antidikos is a courtroom word: the opponent in a lawsuit, the prosecutor. And that is a precise description of what these readers were experiencing — they were being accused, publicly and continuously.

'Prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.' The picture is hunting, and notice what a roaring lion is doing. A lion stalking prey is silent; the roar comes to panic the herd and drive something out of it. The noise is a weapon, and it works on the nerves rather than the body.

'Seeking someone' — the hunt is selective. He is looking for the one that has drifted from the group, which is exactly what persecution does to a congregation.

'Resist him, firm in your faith.' The command is to stand, not to attack. And 'firm' is a solid word — settled, not moving — which is the opposite of the scattering the roar is designed to produce.

Then the encouragement, and it is unexpectedly practical: 'knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.' Not a promise of relief but of company. Isolation is the lion's method, and the answer is the knowledge that you are one of many — which is why Peter wrote a circular letter to five provinces rather than a private note.

verseByVerse.quote: And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And after you have suffered a little while.' Peter does not remove the suffering from the sentence. It stands, and it is bounded — a little while, the same phrase as 1:6, measured against the eternal glory in the next clause.

'The God of all grace.' The title is chosen for the moment. Not the God of all power, though he is; the God of all grace — every kind of it, sufficient for every situation these scattered congregations were in.

'Who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ.' The calling looks past the suffering to the destination, and the destination is his own glory. Peter said in verse 1 that he is a partaker of it; here he says they are called to it.

Then four verbs, and they build: 'will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you.'

Restore is the mending word — used of setting a broken bone and of repairing nets, which Peter had done for a living. It assumes damage: the suffering will break something, and God will set it. Confirm means to make firm, the word the Lord used when he told Peter that after turning again he should strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32). Strengthen is to fill with strength. And establish is to lay on a foundation — to ground something so it cannot be shifted.

And the emphatic word is 'himself'. Not through an agency or a process. God will personally do the mending — which is the promise a battered congregation needed, and it comes from a man who had been broken and repaired by name.

'To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.' Peter has just named the prowling lion; he ends by saying whose the dominion actually is.

verseByVerse.quote: By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son. Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you.' Silvanus is the Silas of Acts — Paul's companion through Philippi and Thessalonica, a Roman citizen, and now carrying Peter's letter. He may have been the letter's scribe as well as its courier, which would account for the polished Greek of a Galilean fisherman.

'Exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it.' That is Peter's own summary of what he has written, and it repays notice. After five chapters on suffering, submission and slander, he calls the whole thing grace. Not advice, not endurance training. Grace — and their part is simply to stand in it.

'She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings.' 'She' is almost certainly the church there, and 'Babylon' is almost certainly Rome. Jewish writers of the period used the name for the great pagan power that had destroyed Jerusalem, and Revelation does the same.

It is a fitting last image for this letter. Peter writes to exiles from the empire's capital and calls it Babylon — the place of exile — reminding them that the church at the centre of the world is as much in a foreign country as the church in Bithynia. And 'likewise chosen' hands them back the word he opened with (1:1).

'And so does Mark, my son.' John Mark — the young man who abandoned Paul and Barnabas, was restored, and by early tradition wrote his Gospel from Peter's preaching. 'My son' is affection, not paternity.

Must Christians greet each other with a kiss today? The point is warm, holy affection between brothers and sisters, expressed in the form one’s culture uses. Where a kiss carries that meaning it may be used; elsewhere a handshake or an embrace obeys the command.

'Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.' The letter that has spoken so much of hostility ends with an instruction to touch each other, and with peace — offered to people who had very little of it, from a man who would shortly die in the city he calls Babylon.
verseByVerse.note: Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. “Babylon” is very probably a code name for Rome. Mark is John Mark, whom early tradition links with Peter as the source of Mark’s Gospel.
